**Case Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 76-year-old South Asian man, a retired electrician who still takes on small repair jobs for neighbors. He has been married to his wife, Sunita, for forty-eight years. He presents with a quiet, measured demeanor, his hands resting flat on his knees as he speaks. He describes himself as a practical man, someone who "fixes things," but his voice falters when he recounts the morning that changed everything.

The event occurred four months ago. Mr. A. was walking to the local hardware store to buy a new fuse box for a client. It was 8:30 AM, a bright, ordinary Tuesday. As he turned down a side alley—a shortcut he had taken for thirty years—a young man stepped out from behind a dumpster. Mr. A. remembers the glint of a knife, the man’s voice telling him to hand over his wallet. He complied immediately. He gave the man his wallet, his watch, and the small tool pouch he carried. The man shoved him to the ground, hard. Mr. A.’s hip struck the pavement. He remembers the cold of the concrete through his trousers, the smell of damp garbage, the sound of the man’s footsteps running away. He lay there for a long moment, not because he was hurt, but because he could not make his body move. A woman found him, helped him up, called the police. He was not seriously injured. The police took a report. The man was never caught.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. A. tried to return to his normal life. He finished the fuse box job. He went to temple with Sunita. But something had shifted. He began to notice that his mind would not stay in the present. While soldering a wire, he would suddenly see the knife, feel the pressure of the man’s hand on his chest. His hands would shake, and he would have to stop. He started avoiding the side streets. Then he started avoiding walking anywhere at all. Now, Sunita drives him to every job, even if it is only two blocks away. He feels a tightness in his chest when he sees a young man in a hooded jacket. He crosses the street. He has not been back to the hardware store.

Sleep has become a battleground. He is exhausted, but his mind will not quiet. He lies awake, replaying the moment: the glint, the voice, the fall. When he does sleep, he dreams of being chased through the alleys of his childhood in Mumbai, the same cold fear in his throat. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart pounding, and lies still, afraid to wake Sunita. He has stopped going to the temple. He cannot sit still through the prayers. Every time he closes his eyes, he sees the alley.

He is irritable, a quality Sunita has never seen in him. He snapped at her last week when she asked him if he wanted tea. He felt immediate shame, but the anger had already left his mouth. He feels disconnected from his own life. He tells me he feels like he is watching himself from a distance—a man who used to fix things, now unable to fix this. He feels a deep, gnawing guilt. He should have fought back. He should have seen the man coming. He should have taken a different route. He repeats these thoughts like a mantra.

His work has suffered. He can still do the technical work—his hands know the wires—but he cannot handle the social part. He cannot meet new clients. He declines jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods. He has lost three regular customers because he cannot bring himself to explain why he will not come to their homes. He feels a constant, low-grade dread, a sense that the world is no longer safe. He checks the locks on his doors three times before bed. He keeps a heavy wrench next to his side of the bed, a tool he used to use for work, now a weapon.

He sits in my office, his hands still on his knees. He does not cry. He tells me he just wants to feel normal again. He wants to walk to the hardware store. He wants to sleep through the night. He wants to stop feeling like a stranger in his own skin. He looks at me, and for a moment, I see the exhaustion of a man who has been trying to fix a broken circuit with no diagram, no tools, and no idea where the fault lies.
